person.name: Zebang Wu
person.headline: Curious about how things work. Interested in what they can become.
person.intro: I’m an Electronic Information Engineering undergraduate at Westlake University. I work across machine learning, simulation, and interactive products, with a growing interest in how people learn and use intelligent systems.

projects.title: Fire, heat & structural damage
projects.subtitle: An interactive starting point for my graduation project.
projects.status: Planned graduation project · prototype in development
projects.summary: Exploring how a thermal field, component temperature, and accumulated damage can be made inspectable in an interactive simulation.

sections.title: From exploration to a graduation project
sections.body: This work is becoming my undergraduate graduation project. The current prototype brings a changing thermal field, component heating, and cumulative damage into one interactive environment, providing a starting point for a more rigorous investigation.

sections.title: Making a process visible
sections.body: The prototype lets a viewer inspect how a thermal process develops over time and how components respond. Its purpose at this stage is to make relationships and behavior visible enough to explore, compare, and discuss.

sections.title: Current scope
sections.body: The model currently uses simplified, uncalibrated demonstration parameters. Its visual behavior has not been physically validated, and it should be read as an exploratory prototype rather than a predictive engineering system.

projects.dateNote: A prototype is recorded in September 2026. Graduation-project direction confirmed by the author on October 1, 2026.

projects.title: InVolve
projects.subtitle: Designing the interaction between a lesson, a teacher, and a classroom.
projects.summary: Classroom interaction software for higher education. I lead the frontend, UI, and interaction design; my collaborator develops the backend.

sections.title: A workflow built around teaching
sections.body: InVolve brings lesson preparation, live classroom interaction, and response review into a connected workflow. The teacher interface is organized around Design, Teach, and Assess, with Prepare, Engage, and Practice phases within the lesson.

sections.title: My contribution
sections.body: I am primarily responsible for the frontend, UI, and interaction design. My work includes the teaching interface, question and question-set organization, student preview, and the transitions between preparing and distributing classroom content. A collaborator is responsible for backend development.

sections.title: Keeping classroom state understandable
sections.body: Draft questions stay out of the student lesson view until they are distributed. Student preview gives teachers a way to inspect the receiving experience, while question organization and statistics entry points help connect preparation, participation, and review.

sections.title: Used in my own course
sections.body: I created and delivered an introductory course on coding with AI agents through InVolve for people with no previous coding experience. This provided a real teaching context for the product, connecting my interface work with the task of helping beginners take their first steps.

projects.dateNote: Development dates are not yet established. A saved course record is from spring 2026.

projects.title: VLA models in the driving loop
projects.subtitle: Connecting model inference to reliable autonomous-driving evaluation.
projects.role: R&D Intern · Dongfeng Motor Corporation R&D Institute
projects.summary: Integrated a vision-language-action model into Bench2Drive/CARLA and worked on the performance and reliability of its closed-loop evaluation pipeline.

sections.title: Integration is part of the experiment
sections.body: I integrated a vision-language-action model with Bench2Drive and CARLA for closed-loop evaluation. This required correcting trajectory coordinates and navigation mappings, and synchronizing camera inputs with ego-vehicle history so the model and simulator described the same state.

sections.title: Tracing inference overhead
sections.body: I identified and removed redundant multi-gigabyte array copies in the ONNX inference path. A route-level benchmark recorded approximately 68 seconds of baseline mean latency and 5.7 seconds of optimized warm-state median latency. These use different summary statistics and operating conditions, so they are reported as observations rather than a universal speedup ratio.

sections.title: Making evaluation recoverable
sections.body: I built a persistent PyTorch inference service and a resumable evaluation pipeline. Isolating simulator and model dependencies helped make the system easier to operate and diagnose, while distinguishing driving failures from simulator and evaluation faults made the resulting evidence more interpretable.

projects.title: Reconstruction beyond one sensor path
projects.subtitle: Baseline evaluation under changes in sensing trajectories.
projects.summary: Comparing physical-field reconstruction baselines when sensors follow trajectories different from the original sensing distribution.

sections.title: The evaluation question
sections.body: A reconstruction method can perform differently when the sensing trajectory changes. My work examines this shift through baseline comparisons, using shared evaluation protocols to make the behavior of different methods comparable.

sections.title: My contribution
sections.body: I evaluated randomized-trajectory fine-tuning and empirical Gaussian-process methods, and compared reconstruction errors across scan and rotated trajectories. My contribution is centered on these baseline experiments and their analysis, rather than ownership of the overall paper method.

sections.title: Reading the trade-off
sections.body: The comparison considers both adaptation to new trajectories and performance on the original sensing distribution. This makes the trade-off visible: an adaptation strategy needs to be assessed for what it gains under a new trajectory and what it may lose under the original one.

projects.evidenceStatus: Personal contribution: baseline comparisons; paper status and authorship not asserted

projects.title: AI support for family care
projects.subtitle: Turning family needs into product requirements and interactive prototypes.
projects.summary: Product exploration for a family-care robot, spanning requirements, account permissions, AI conversations, scheduling prototypes, and technology research.

sections.title: Starting with the family
sections.body: I translate eldercare and family-support needs into product requirements and user journeys. The interaction work includes account permissions, AI conversations, and emergency-contact flows, connecting a family situation to the actions and information the product needs to support.

sections.title: Making workflows tangible
sections.body: I built Vue and TypeScript prototypes and a local scheduling service with seven MCP tools. Synthetic data, version-conflict checks, and retry handling allowed AI-assisted workflows to be demonstrated while exploring how the system should respond to changing or interrupted requests.

sections.title: Research that informs decisions
sections.body: I evaluated health-sensing and audio-service vendors, and organized 27 health-management sources into a searchable reference library. This work supports product design and integration planning; the prototypes are described as prototypes, without implying that every capability has been deployed.

projects.title: Listening to student well-being
projects.subtitle: A qualitative study with Deaf and Hard-of-Hearing students.
projects.summary: A faculty-supervised study of Deaf and Hard-of-Hearing students’ well-being, from interview design and fieldwork coordination to thematic analysis and writing.

sections.title: Understanding lived experience
sections.body: This study approaches student well-being through qualitative research. Working under faculty supervision, I helped turn a broad question about happiness into an interview-based study that could attend to participants’ own accounts.

sections.title: My contribution
sections.body: I led the student research work, designed interviews, coordinated interview arrangements and fieldwork, organized research materials, and conducted thematic analysis. The work involved both keeping the research process moving and interpreting what emerged from it.

sections.title: Writing the study
sections.body: I am the first author of the resulting manuscript. As recorded in my September 2026 résumé, it is under review at Applied Research in Quality of Life. This project is distinct from the related systematic review of AI for Deaf and Hard-of-Hearing people.

projects.dateNote: Manuscript status reflects the September 29, 2026 résumé.

projects.title: Choosing what a model learns next
projects.subtitle: From neural query policies to self-supervised error-reduction sampling.
projects.summary: An investigation of sample selection for neural-operator learning, including neural query strategies and a later error-reduction approach.

sections.title: Beginning with a query policy
sections.body: The early phase explored neural-network-based query strategies for selecting useful training samples in a continuous sample space. The work connected sample selection with the behavior of the model being trained, and exposed questions about data requirements and continual learning.

sections.title: Moving toward error reduction
sections.body: I subsequently developed self-supervised error-reduction sampling. My résumé documents evaluation on an MLP-based DeepONet for Burgers’ equation, with attention to how the sampling approach affected learning.

sections.title: What the experiments asked
sections.body: The analysis considered sample efficiency alongside computational cost and continual-learning limitations. The two phases belong to one research trajectory: an initial strategy, the constraints it exposed, and a revised approach to choosing training data.

projects.dateNote: The legacy site also contains toy-model and FNO figures; each figure should retain its own experimental context.

projects.title: Relativity you can interact with
projects.subtitle: Connecting scientific accuracy with a VR learning experience.
projects.summary: Research support for teaching special relativity through VR, combining literature review, instructional sequencing, and verification of simulation parameters.

sections.title: From an abstract concept to an experience
sections.body: The project explores how special relativity can be taught through an interactive virtual environment. My work drew on literature about embodiment, agency, and interactivity to inform the research design.

sections.title: My contribution
sections.body: I helped refine the instructional sequence and VR interactions, and verified relativistic parameters in Unity simulations. This connected the intended learning experience with the physical behavior being represented.

sections.title: A research contribution with a defined scope
sections.body: My contribution concerns research design support, instructional interaction, and scientific consistency. The work is presented on those terms, without claiming a measured improvement in learning outcomes.

projects.title: FeasyPaste
projects.subtitle: Keep the ideas. Keep the formatting.
projects.summary: A browser extension for moving LLM responses into Feishu while preserving equations, code blocks, and lists.

sections.title: A small but persistent frustration
sections.body: An answer can be useful and still become difficult to use when copying it into another editor breaks its equations, numbering, or code. FeasyPaste addresses this handoff between an LLM response and a Feishu document.

sections.title: The product
sections.body: I independently developed the extension to convert LLM output into Feishu-compatible formatting. Its focus is a short, practical workflow: copy an answer and preserve the structure that makes it readable.

sections.title: Designed around a concrete task
sections.body: The project is intentionally focused on a recurring task. It reflects my interest in building small tools that remove repeated friction from learning and working with AI.

projects.dateNote: March 2026 is a store-version reference, not a confirmed development start date.

sections.title: Organizing a body of rules

sections.title: My contribution
sections.body: I independently developed the site. The project brings together website development, information organization, and a learning-oriented presentation of the material.

projects.title: Material behavior under constraints
projects.subtitle: Learning to build mechanical simulations around physical boundary conditions.
projects.summary: Research exploration of material creep and mechanics, including Abaqus and crystal-symmetry boundary conditions.

sections.title: Working with a physical model
sections.body: This work introduced me to mechanical simulation at the lattice scale and to the practical use of Abaqus. It expanded my research experience beyond model training into setting up physically constrained simulations.

sections.title: My contribution
sections.body: I worked on applying crystal-symmetry boundary conditions through coupling constraints. The experience emphasized how the definition of a simulation, including its boundaries, shapes the behavior it can meaningfully represent.

projects.dateNote: The legacy site records work beginning in July 2025; an end date is not established.

projects.title: Wav2Vec ASR experiments
projects.subtitle: Preparing data for a model is part of building the model.
projects.summary: Deployment and fine-tuning experiments with Wav2Vec, including Python-based data cleaning and relabeling.

sections.title: The experiment
sections.body: I worked on deploying and fine-tuning an automatic speech-recognition model. The experience involved understanding the model’s expectations and preparing data to fit its training setup.

sections.title: My contribution
sections.body: I used Python to clean and relabel data and worked through the experimental pipeline. This was an early encounter with the close relationship between data preparation and model behavior.

sections.title: My contribution

projects.subtitle: Teaching beginners to take their first steps with coding agents.
projects.summary: I created and taught an introduction to coding with AI agents for people with no prior programming experience, using InVolve.

sections.title: Starting from zero
sections.body: The course was designed for people who had no prior coding experience. Its focus was using an AI coding agent to begin working with code, with explanations and exercises delivered through InVolve.

sections.title: Teaching with a tool I helped build
sections.body: I created the course and taught it through InVolve. This joined two responsibilities: shaping the learning material, and using the classroom interactions that I had worked on as the product’s frontend and interaction designer.

sections.title: A concrete teaching artifact
sections.body: The saved lesson includes written explanations, an exercise, and illustrated material. It provides a real teaching case alongside the software project, without treating sample classroom responses as evidence of actual student outcomes.

projects.role: President · College Student Union, Westlake University
projects.summary: Organized six campus events for 30–300 attendees each and introduced recurring reports and handover summaries.

sections.title: From planning to participation
sections.body: As president of the College Student Union, I organized six campus events, with each serving roughly 30 to 300 attendees. The role involved coordinating preparation and keeping the team’s work moving toward a shared event.

sections.title: Building continuity
sections.body: I introduced biweekly reports and term-end handover summaries. These practices made ongoing work easier to follow and helped the next group inherit more than a list of unfinished tasks.

sections.title: A widening set of questions

projects.summary: An exchange semester that extended my engineering studies and connected them with research in VR and learning.

sections.body: I spent an exchange semester in Cornell’s College of Engineering as an Electrical & Computer Engineering student. The experience broadened the academic settings and disciplines through which I approached engineering.

projects.subtitle: A place for thoughts that do not fit a résumé.
projects.summary: Personal notes, conversations with AI, visual work, and an interest in literature and the experience of learning.

sections.title: Writing as a way of thinking
sections.body: My existing website includes “Abandon,” an exchange with an AI assistant about memory, continuity, and unfinished work. My question and the AI-generated response are attributed separately. The writing section also leaves room for future personal essays and reflections.

sections.title: Beyond the project list
sections.body: I enjoy literature, visual design, music, and cycling. A preference for clear lines, warm greens and yellows, orange, and a little fox-like playfulness also informs how I want this website to feel.
